summary: At 1,785 square miles, El Dorado County is larger than Rhode Island yet holds fewer than 193,000 people — a density of just 108 per square mile that reflects a landscape climbing from the oak-studded foothills east of Sacramento all the way up to the Sierra Nevada crest at Lake Tahoe. That geography defines daily life: the western half, anchored by Placerville and the Highway 50 corridor, sits in rolling gold-country terrain with warm, dry summers averaging 64°F highs and over nine hours of daily sunshine, while the eastern reaches climb into genuine alpine country with ski resorts and granite peaks. The county functions substantially as a bedroom community; many commuters head west on U.S. 50 toward Sacramento, a drive that can stretch well past an hour during peak traffic — a real cost baked into the lifestyle. A median home value of $640,500 against a median household income of $106,190 yields a price-to-income ratio around 6:1, meaningful but notably less punishing than coastal California metros. The property crime rate of roughly 1,150 per 100,000 sits well below the statewide average. Government, healthcare, and tourism form the employment backbone, with limited corporate headquarters or large private-sector campuses, so switching jobs without switching counties is genuinely constrained. What you get instead is direct access to the American River canyon, El Dorado National Forest, and Desolation Wilderness — serious outdoor infrastructure, not decorative greenbelts. El Dorado is essentially a place where the commute subsidizes the setting, and whether that arithmetic works depends entirely on how much you value a trailhead over a short drive to the office.
